title: Sita in the fire: two Ramayanas
hookLine: two tellings of Sita, and the argument people have about them
carry: many ramayanas, and sita is never ravana's
tomorrow: a fish, a tortoise, a boar: why is a row of animals one god?

lines: WHICH VERSION IS THE REAL ONE?
cards: Every fandom has the fight over which version is the real one. Rama's story has one too.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana, which tradition places in the Brahmanda Purana, Shiva tells Rama's story to Parvati, and it runs the familiar road: the exile, the forest, the golden deer.
Then, just before Ravana comes, Rama asks Sita to go into the fire for safekeeping and leave a likeness of herself behind. The Sita that Ravana carries off to Lanka is the likeness.
The real Sita waits, untouched, until the fire gives her back.

teach.b: Adhyatma means having to do with the self, the inner side of things. This telling keeps pausing so someone can say who Rama really is: the supreme Self, come in a human life, with Sita as his shakti, his own power.
The likeness fits that. In Valmiki's Ramayana, though, the Sita Ravana takes is Sita herself. So people who love this story weigh the two tellings, and both sides have a real case.
Here's the first, at its best. Sita is the goddess.

teach.h: CASE ONE: NOTHING CAN TOUCH HER.
teach.b: Nothing Ravana does can touch her, and the likeness says so in story form. It spares her, it spares the devotee who can't bear to picture her a prisoner, and it fits a book whose whole point is the truth under the events.
Now the second, at its best. In Valmiki, the real Sita is taken, and she stays herself: she refuses Ravana, she waits, she holds on in a garden full of guards.

teach.h: CASE TWO: HER COURAGE IS THE POINT.
teach.b: Her courage is the point. A likeness, this side says, takes away the very thing that makes her a hero.

teach.h: MANY RAMAYANAS. SITA IS NEVER RAVANA'S.
teach.b: And notice what the two sides agree on: Sita is never Ravana's. That's the teaching under both. Many Hindus worship Sita as Lakshmi come to earth, Rama's own power, and no Ravana can own her.
And there was never just one Ramayana: the tradition keeps many tellings, side by side.

how: The Adhyatma Ramayana is read and recited by some Rama devotees, especially for its hymns and its teaching passages; Valmiki's Ramayana and many other tellings are read alongside it.

o: a retelling of Rama's story set inside a giant egg
the Purana of Brahma's egg, home of an inner Ramayana
the egg Sita hides in while Ravana searches Lanka

s: in every Ramayana, Ravana carries off the real Sita
in the Adhyatma Ramayana he takes a likeness; the real Sita waits in the fire.
in the Adhyatma Ramayana, Shiva tells the story to Parvati
that's its frame: Rama's story, told by Shiva to Parvati.
readers of the Adhyatma think Valmiki's Sita is fake
the tradition keeps both tellings, and some readers read both.

games.q: your friend loves the Adhyatma's likeness. state the other side's best case in one line.
o: in Valmiki, the real Sita is taken and stays herself; her courage is the point.
the likeness is newer, so it can't be authentic.
the likeness makes Sita weaker than Ravana.
games.why: that's the Valmiki side at its best: a Sita who is really there, refusing Ravana and holding on. both sides agree she is never his.

practice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Think of something you and someone close to you see differently, and write their side in one sentence, as well as they'd put it themselves. Read it back once, slowly, and let it stand.
If you pray, you can hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: The Brahmanda: the Purana of Brahma's egg, where tradition places a Ramayana told from the inside.

orig.note: Sanskrit adhyatma: having to do with the self, the inner side. It names this Ramayana.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: many Ramayanas, and Sita is never Ravana's. Until tomorrow.
